subject: Re: Memory allocation playbook — Omniscience Therapeutics (long-context sizing)

Subject: Sizing worksheet request — long context (64k)

Hi Monica,

Thanks again for last week's demo. We have internal stakeholders asking for a concrete sizing worksheet so procurement can scope the PO. High level requirements:
- Model: custom-finetuned Llama-70B variant (sparse adapters)
- Typical request pattern: 30 concurrent interactive sessions, median prompt+response ~ 6k tokens, peak up to 64k context windows for batch analytics jobs (rare, 5% of requests)
- SLO: 1500ms p50 for interactive, burst to 60 concurrent for 15 minutes during experiments
- Preference for Dedicated capacity (reserved pods) with a fallback to a smaller quantized variant on lower-memory GPUs for overflow

Can you send a playbook that maps model/context profiles to GPU pod configurations and the expected cost delta if we keep a 1.25x headroom buffer? Also, what’s the quantization/behavior tradeoff for our finetuned model vs. the base?

Attachment: example_omniscience_workload.csv (simple traffic distribution)

Best,
Sylvia

Subject: Re: Sizing worksheet request — long context (64k)

Hi Sylvia —

Thanks for the detail and the sample traffic. I attached a first-pass playbook (omniscience_dedicated_playbook_v1.xlsx) and a short model-variant summary as PDF. High-level recommendations below; see worksheet for line-by-line math.

Summary recommendations (executive):
- Primary fleet: 3 reserved pods of H100-80GB (each pod = 4 GPUs) configured for the full-precision finetuned 70B-64k runpath. This supports ~30 steady concurrent interactive sessions with 1.25x headroom and allows the 64k KV cache to reside in local HBM without offload for p50 latency targets.
- Overflow / burst policy: allow routing to quantized-4bit variants (Redwood Q4F) on smaller 40–48GB cards (A100-40 / H100-40 equivalent). Maintain 2 hot-standby pods for burst capacity (can be preemptible).
- Canaries and rollouts: start with 1 pod in dedicated + 1 quantized pod in warm standby for the first month to validate quality impact.

Key sizing notes (technical):
- Model memory baseline (approx): Llama-70B in FP16 -> ~140GB model RAM footprint; model sharding across 4x 80GB GPUs reduces per-device residency to ~35GB leaving ~45GB HBM for KV cache and activations.
- KV cache for 64k context: worst-case working set (single request) grows roughly linearly with context length; plan ~40–60GB of KV per concurrent long-context session depending on token packing and sequence-parallel layout. For your typical distribution (few long requests), proactive prefix caching + request routing keeps average KV residency lower.
- Headroom: we use a 1.25x factor on steady concurrency to handle bursts and model overhead (tracing, small evals).

Quantization tradeoffs:
- Q4F (4-bit fine-tuned) reduces model residency by ~2.5–3x in practice, enabling serving on 40–48GB cards for stateless inference. However, KV cache remains dense and still requires HBM — long-context batch jobs that rely on exact KV semantics will see small fidelity regressions (~1–3% measured on our eval set) while latency decreases by ~20–35%.
- Recommended policy: route interactive low-latency traffic to Q4F when the response length is <8k tokens to save cost; reserve FP16 pods for long-context batches and experiments.

Operational items / attachments:
- Attached playbook contains per-model per-precision pod counts, GPU hours estimates, and a staged rollout timeline (Week 0–4).
- I included an example routing policy snippet (in the sheet) you can drop into Redwood Console for canary + overflow routing.

Next steps: if this aligns, I can convert the worksheet into a PO-ready commitment table and an SLO appendix for legal.

Thanks — looping Karthik and Marcus for final technical confirmation below.

— Monica
Monica Patel
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>, Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-09-12T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Sizing worksheet request — technical confirmation and pod breakdown

Monica / Marcus —

Reviewed the worksheet. A couple of clarifications and an alternative pod topology to present to the customer:

1) Alternative pod split (cost vs latency):
   - Conservative (low-risk): 3x H100-80 pods (4x GPUs each) + 2x standby H100-80 for scheduled experiments. Pros: minimal offload, consistent p50; Cons: higher committed cost.
   - Hybrid (recommended): 2x H100-80 pods (reserved) sized for steady interactive + 2x A100-40 pods reserved for quantized overflow. Add autoscale policy to spin additional A100-40 preemptible pods for short experiments (15–30 min). This reduces committed GPU hours by ~22% in our estimates.

2) KV cache accounting:
   - For your request mix, assume 30 concurrent sessions with 3 long-context sessions active simultaneously during experiments. Use per-token KV delta we measured on similar 70B builds: ~0.9KB/token (including keys+values+overheads) after packing and attention optimizations. At 64k tokens, that equates to ~57.6GB per long request. With 3 parallel long requests you need ~175GB KV working set — split across the pod's aggregate HBM. That drives the need for multi-GPU pods rather than single 80GB cards.

3) Quantization behavior on finetuned adapters:
   - Our internal eval shows the adapter parameters are robust to Q4F if we keep adapter layers in higher precision (a mixed-precision config). That keeps downstream task degradation under 2% on average for your eval prompts. We'll document the exact adapter-to-base precision mapping in the final playbook.

4) Suggested routing policy example for Redwood Console (brief):
   - Route by expected response length + label: if expected_response_tokens > 12k -> route to FP16 reserved pods; else route to Q4F pool. During bursts, route non-SLA traffic to preemptible quantized pods.

I'll update the sheet with the hybrid pod cost delta and the per-pod KV distribution. Marcus, can you sanity-check the per-token KV figure and HBM split?

Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
